memories.line: The sign is gone. I am selling the blade as what it is. People still buy good steel.
'Patterned blade, Emberford steel.' Fewer words on the sign. More buyers, strangely.
I put a note under the sign, as the crowd asked. People read it before they read me.
My sign is still up. Come back with better cards, Guardian. I will be here.
It took you a few weighings? Good. The beam is patient, and so is the guild.
The found weight is in the guild box now, with a tag: FOUR, NOT FIVE.
The brass door flickered at you first, I hear. It flickers at me too, some days.
You opened the Timeline Door. Not many notice that a date can be a date of telling.
After you left, I read the record book myself. Next time I will start there.
I told three people what the record says. One of them believed me. That is a start.
Tea, Guardian? I now say 'I heard' before I pass a story on. It slows me down. Good.
Your test billet is still by my anvil. Light and dark layers, and you made them.
The catalogue says the ingots are 'probably' eighteenth century. 'Probably' is an honest word.
Both streets count the same knots on the rope now. Fewer arguments at dawn.
I saw your yarn on the practice board. The gold ones were pulled tight!
You gave me a fair point in front of everyone. I have thought about it since.
You sat by the Waystone for a while. Good. The market will still be here.
Your new pen label is clearer than the first one. Now I can tell what each 'first' was about.
I read your pen label twice. 'First' meant a different thing for each pen. I did not know that.
I walked the Hall of Firsts. Each plaque says what kind of first it was: first to do it, first to publish it, first we know of.
Your claim board has a counterclaim on it. Good. A board with only one side is a poster, not research.
Your Glimmermoth landed on my ledger. It went straight to the page I touch most.
The bare carving is beautiful. I do miss the gold, a little. Nobody now living painted it, and nobody can paint it back.
The gold is bright again, and the carving waits under it. A restorer in fifty years can still choose differently.
Every child who reads the gate now asks: why do the two plaques say different things? That is the best question in Emberford.
The plaque looks new. Your label is the only thing that remembers what is under the paint. I keep a copy in the ledger.
Ysolde! My grandmother had an aunt called Ysolde. No, I cannot prove it is the same one. But I like the name on the gate.
I read your label on the gate. 'Which words belong to which time': I will use that in my own catalogue.
I only said a boy picked up a pot. By lunch it was 'a gang of thieves'. Thank you for writing what I actually saw.
The guild fixed the loose stone this morning. Your report did that, not my shouting.
I told everyone about the boy as if I had seen him. I had not. I heard it from Mara. I will say so next time.
We dug at the low place on your map. Water at nine knots down. The town will have its third well by winter.
The new children found the echo on the first day! I want to add a seventh layer: places where you can hear the bells.
My green apples go to market again. Mara said sorry, and the sorter did not have to. Funny, that.
Every new season I put one of each new fruit in the example tray. Pears next week. I will test it first.
We cut the footbridge rope to your measure, with a little extra. A good measurer always adds a little extra, and says so.
The council read your survey. They asked the night porters too, this time. I was very surprised to be asked.
Tova sent a slate back: 'Tavi did well.' You, and we. My grandmother would like your translation.
Nell says the fair poster is the best one. I asked to hang the whole painting in the hall as well. People should see the old stall too.
Noa says you kept the board well. Not always right, she says: honest about how sure you were. That is rarer.
